[[File:Kaufman Mall and the Webb University Center.JPG|thumb|The Webb University Center of [[Old Dominion University]] viewed from Kaufman Mall, completed in 1966.]]
'''William Marshall Jr.''' {{post-nominals|list=[[FAIA]]}} (1925–1997) was an American [[architect]] in practice in [[Norfolk, Virginia]] from 1955 to 1984 and was president of the [[American Institute of Architects]] for 1975.

==Life and career==
William Marshall Jr. was born November 24, 1925, in [[Ashland, Kentucky]] to William Marshall, a civil engineer, and Lee (Powers) Marshall.<ref name="Marquis">"Marshall, William Jr." in ''Who's Who in America'' (New Providence: Marquis Who's Who, 1992): 2193.</ref> The family moved to [[Virginia]] shortly thereafter and in 1939 settled permanently in [[Norfolk, Virginia|Norfolk]]. In 1943 he enrolled in the [[Virginia Military Institute]] to study engineering, but left in 1944 to enlist in the [[United States Army]]. After the war he enrolled in the [[University of Virginia]] to study architecture, and graduated with a BS in architecture in 1949. He then enrolled in the MArch program at [[Columbia University]] but dropped out after a year to begin work. In 1950 he returned to Norfolk, where he joined the office of Lublin, McGaughy & Associates, architects and engineers, and in 1955 he became a partner. In 1960 the senior partner, Alfred M. Lublin, died, and Marshall became senior architect of the firm.<ref name="Vosbeck"/> The firm's practice expanded quickly, and by 1962 they had offices in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]], [[Honolulu]], [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]], [[Paris]], [[Livorno]] and [[Wiesbaden]] in addition to the head office in Norfolk.<ref>"Lublin, McGaughy & Associates" in ''American Architects Directory'' (New York: R. R. Bowker Company, 1962): 434.</ref> In 1965 the firm was reorganized as McGaughy, Marshall & McMillan.<ref name="Marshall70"/> By 1970 they had centralized their foreign practice in an office in [[Athens]] with stateside offices in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]], [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond]], [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha]] and [[Grand Island, Nebraska|Grand Island]]<ref>"McGaughy, Marshall & McMillan" in ''American Architects Directory'' (New York: R. R. Bowker Company, 1970): 576.</ref> and in 1981 reorganized as the MMM Design Group with Marshall as president.<ref>Virginia corporation records</ref> In addition to conventional architectural and engineering practice, the firm was responsible for master plans for new towns and cities in [[Africa]] and [[Asia]].<ref name="Vosbeck"/> Marshall retired in 1984 but continued to maintain a small consulting practice from an office in [[Exmore, Virginia|Exmore]]. MMM Design Group survived his retirement by thirty years, but faltered during the [[Great Recession]] and ultimately closed in 2014.<ref>Reynolds Hutchins, "[https://www.pilotonline.com/inside-business/article_eae98f48-6805-5aea-a2e5-a76a53abc428.html After nearly 70 years, MMM Design firm closes]," Virginian–Pilot, October 17, 2014. Accessed March 9, 2023.</ref>

Marshall joined the [[American Institute of Architects]] (AIA) in 1958 as a member of the Virginia chapter. He served as chapter president for 1969–70 and was a member of several national committees. In 1971 when AIA vice president [[George Malcolm White]] was appointed [[Architect of the Capitol]], Marshall was appointed to finish his term. In 1973 he was elected first vice president/president elect for 1974 and president for 1975. As president Marshall focused on strengthening local and state chapters and during the [[1970s energy crisis|energy crisis]] advocated for energy efficiency in design and construction. Marshall was elected a [[Fellow of the American Institute of Architects|fellow]] of the AIA in 1972 and was elected an honorary member of the [[Royal Architectural Institute of Canada]].<ref name="Vosbeck">R. Randall Vosbeck, ''A Legacy of Leadership: The Presidents of the American Institute of Architects, 1857–2007'' (Washington: American Institute of Architects, 2008): 133–136.</ref>

==Personal life==
Marshall was married in 1951 to Joan Goodyear Ellingston. They had five children, three sons and two daughters.<ref name="Marquis"/> Marshall died November 8, 1997, in Norfolk at the age of 71.<ref name="Vosbeck"/>

==Architectural works==
* Southern Shopping Center, 7525 Tidewater Dr, [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1957)<ref name="Marshall62">"Marshall, William Jr." in ''American Architects Directory'' (New York: R. R. Bowker Company, 1962): 464.</ref>
* Master plan and buildings, [[Joint Forces Staff College]], [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1958)<ref name="Marshall62"/>
* Chesapeake Municipal Center,{{efn|name=Civic|Bernard B. Spigel, architect; Lublin, McGaughy & Associates, associate architect. Originally intended as the Civic Center of [[Norfolk County, Virginia|Norfolk County]] which became the city of Chesapeake in 1963.}} 306 Cedar Rd, [[Chesapeake, Virginia]] (1961, altered)<ref name="Marshall62"/>
* Kirn Memorial Library, 301 E City Hall Ave, [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1962, demolished 2009)<ref>Richard Guy Wilson, ''Buildings of Virginia: Tidewater and Piedmont'' (New York: Oxford University Press, 2002)</ref>
* [[Embassy of Germany, Washington, D.C.|Embassy of Germany]],{{efn|name=Germany|[[Egon Eiermann]], architect; Lublin, McGaughy & Associates, associate architect.}} 4645 Reservoir Rd NW, [[Washington, D.C.]] (1964)<ref name="Vosbeck"/>
* Algonquin House, 7320 Glenroie Ave, [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1965)<ref name="Marshall70">"Marshall, William Jr." in ''American Architects Directory'' (New York: R. R. Bowker Company, 1970): 597.</ref>
* Webb University Center, [[Old Dominion University]], [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1966)<ref name="Marshall70"/>
* BB&T Building, 500 E Main St, [[Norfolk, Virginia]] (1970)<ref name="Marquis"/>
* Master plan of [[Marj]], [[Libya]] (1970)<ref name="Vosbeck"/>
* [[Ministry of Defense (Saudi Arabia)|Ministry of Defense]] headquarters, [[Riyadh]], [[Saudi Arabia]] (1976)<ref name="Marquis"/>
* Nebraska East Union, [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] East Campus, [[Lincoln, Nebraska]] (1977)<ref>"Union in 'Central' Spot," ''Lincoln Star'', February 20, 1977, 2N.</ref>
* Master plan of [[Brega]], [[Libya]] (1980)<ref name="Marquis"/>
* [[Old Post Office (Washington, D.C.)|Old Post Office]] rehabilitation,{{efn|name=PO|[[Arthur Cotton Moore]]/Associates, architect; McGaughy, Marshall & McMillan, associate architect.}} 1100 Pennsylvania Ave NW, [[Washington, D.C.]] (1983)<ref>G. Martin Moeller Jr., ''AIA Guide to the Architecture of Washington, D.C.'' (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012)</ref>
* Master plan of [[Hamad Town]], [[Bahrain]] (1984)<ref>"Export Opportunities" in ''Business America'' 6, no. 10 (May 16, 1983): 36.</ref>
